rationale: Honeybee colonies normally have a queen, not multiple kings; workers may kill or supersede queens and destroy queen cells, but the statement misidentifies sex and overstates the behavior.
Bees often show floral constancy during a foraging trip, but it is a tendency rather than an invariant rule and they can switch flower species before returning.
Documented human births have included more than five infants at one delivery, so the asserted maximum is false.
Honeybee age polyethism runs in the opposite direction: younger workers usually perform in-hive tasks and older workers forage outside.
Most bony fishes have opercula and most cartilaginous fishes have exposed gill slits, but attributing this directly to a cartilaginous skeleton is unsupported and exceptions exist.
Paired true horns are strongly associated with even-toed ungulates, while living odd-toed or solid-hoofed mammals do not normally bear a pair of true horns.
Dolphins are viviparous mammals with paired mammary slits near the genital region; the nipples are concealed within those slits.
In most insects the male intromittent organ enters the female reproductive tract, although some unusual groups reverse conventional roles.
Hair identifies mammals, but monotremes have hair and lay eggs rather than bearing live young.
Elephants usually bear one calf, but gestation averages roughly 18 to 22 months rather than uniformly two years, and twins occasionally occur.
Male parental guarding of eggs and fry occurs in some sheatfish or catfish, but the exact forty-to-fifty-day duration and described division of labor are species-dependent.
Eels reproduce sexually from eggs; they do not arise spontaneously from worms in putrefying mud.
In cicadas the conspicuous acoustic calling song is produced by males, while females generally respond without comparable song.
Rabies is usually fatal after symptoms and infects many mammals, including humans, but not every bitten animal becomes infected and humans are not an exception.
Hair does not continue biological growth after death; skin dehydration and retraction can merely make it appear longer.
Normal adult tooth counts are not systematically greater in males than females in humans or these livestock species.
Many interspecific hybrids besides mules are sterile or have strongly reduced fertility, and some crosses do not produce viable offspring at all.
Sperm arise from the germ line and carry inherited information; they are not assembled by drawing material from every body part.
Partridges and many other ground-nesting birds perform distraction displays, including feigned injury, to lead predators away from chicks.
Many fishes have very high pre-adult mortality and compensate with large numbers of eggs, though this is not the strategy of every fish.
Octopuses have eight arms, but squid and cuttlefish have eight arms plus two specialized tentacles, so not all cephalopods have only eight feet.
Many bears give birth during winter denning, fast through denning, and emerge with cubs in spring, although dates and complete fasting vary by species and individual.
Scaled fishes include both egg-laying and live-bearing species, while cartilaginous fishes include numerous oviparous skates and sharks; anglerfish are bony fishes.
Eels reproduce sexually, possess gonads and reproductive ducts, and spawn eggs despite the historical difficulty of observing their oceanic reproduction.
Placental viviparity occurs in several sharks, where embryos initially use yolk and later receive maternal support through a uterine placental connection.
Age-related greying occurs in many mammals, including dogs, primates and other species, not practically only humans and horses.
Argonauts can swim and use expanded arm membranes in reproduction and shell formation, but the romantic account of sailing with a membrane and rudder arms is not supported.
Some spider wasps paralyze spiders and provision enclosed nests for larvae, but the broad label, killing rather than paralysis, and mud-wall details do not fit all such wasps.
Humans normally have twelve pairs of ribs, not eight.
Partridges require transfer of sperm for fertilization; wind, voice or breath alone cannot impregnate a female.
The right kidney is higher in some animals, but in humans it is normally lower because of the liver, so the universal claim fails.
A honeybee queen produces both female worker offspring and reproductive offspring, although drones arise from unfertilized eggs and workers influence caste through rearing.
Swans vocalize, but there is no good evidence that they produce a special musical song chiefly before death or fly to sea to do so.
Elephants can use the trunk as a snorkel while crossing water, holding its tip above the surface to breathe.
Humans have a large brain relative to body mass among mammals, but not the largest relative brain across all animals, and 'moistest' is neither established nor a meaningful comparative distinction.
In temperate social wasps, colonies usually die in winter while newly mated queens overwinter in sheltered sites; workers generally do not survive to a second season.
Female octopuses commonly guard and aerate their eggs continuously, cease feeding or feed very little, and deteriorate before dying after brooding.

A worker honeybee often dies after leaving a barbed sting in elastic mammalian skin because abdominal tissues tear, but it can withdraw from some targets and does not invariably die after every sting.
Crocodilians open the mouth mainly by moving the lower jaw relative to the skull, as other jawed vertebrates do; head tilting can create the contrary appearance.
These crustaceans repeatedly molt their exoskeleton as they grow and are soft immediately after ecdysis.
Many mullets move from marine waters into estuaries and rivers, while freshwater eels make the opposite spawning migration to the sea, though species-level patterns vary.
Scorpion young ride on and later disperse from their mother rather than routinely killing her, and spiders likewise show no general offspring-matricide rule.
Many temperate reptiles reduce activity and feeding during winter brumation, but not all listed species do so for exactly four months and crocodiles or tropical forms differ markedly.
Molluscs, tunicates and barnacles develop from sexually or asexually produced propagules; substrate preferences do not imply spontaneous generation from mud or rock.
Not every bird or mammal is infested with lice, and asses can carry both lice and ticks.
Vertebrate brains are richly vascularized and supplied with blood; they are metabolically active rather than universally bloodless and naturally cold.
Several raptors are social or form flocks, especially during migration, communal roosting or cooperative hunting.
The named birds primarily migrate or remain active; swallows do not normally overwinter featherless in holes, although rare torpor occurs in some birds.

Most fishes have separate sexes, but claims that particular named forms are exclusively egg-filled likely confuse species identity, season or unusual reproductive systems and are not generally secure.
Cuckoos are a distinct lineage from hawks and differ anatomically; predation evidence is not logically decisive, but the central denial of transformation is correct.
Many human newborns, especially those with more melanin, do not have bluish eyes, and eye-color changes after birth also occur in other animals.
Typical horned ruminants lack upper incisors, possess a four-compartment stomach and chew cud, though the anatomical correlation is not an exceptionless definition of horned quadrupeds.
Genetic recombination allows traits and resemblance to recur in grandchildren or later descendants even when they are not conspicuous in the intervening generation.
The brain is the principal integrative organ for sensation; its neural tissue processes sensory signals even though direct stimulation of brain tissue may not itself feel painful.
The male octopus hectocotylized arm transfers spermatophores and is specifically adapted for reproduction.
Multiple animals, including some whales, sharks and tortoises, have credible maximum lifespans exceeding those of humans and elephants.
Many pigeons form durable socially monogamous pair bonds, often lasting until death, but extra-pair mating and re-pairing occur.

True horns, tusks and specialized carnassial-like dentitions usually occur in different mammalian lineages, but the universal wording and ambiguous categories make exceptions or definitional counterexamples plausible.
Some kingfishers can breed in winter in suitable climates, but breeding timing varies geographically and is not uniquely fixed to the winter solstice.
Sessile animals commonly reproduce sexually; oysters, barnacles, tunicates and many other attached forms have sexes or are hermaphroditic.
Electric rays generate strong bioelectric discharges used to stun prey and defend themselves, and these shocks can be felt by humans.
Fishes suffer transmissible epidemics caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites, sometimes producing mass mortality.
Fig wasps develop inside receptive figs and transfer pollen between trees; caprification with male or wild figs is used to pollinate certain cultivated figs and promote fruit development.

Castration before maturity suppresses androgen-dependent comb development, crowing and sexual behavior, while castration of adults causes regression of these traits; the precise cautery method is less certain.
The celebrated crocodile-cleaning-bird story lacks strong reliable observation and is not established as a regular mutualism.
Many cuckoos are brood parasites whose chicks are raised by smaller host birds, but laying only one egg and the adult first devouring host eggs are not universal and some cuckoos build nests.
Male sharks and other chondrichthyans possess paired claspers by the pelvic fins, a reliable external sexual distinction absent in females.

Water often retains daytime heat and may be warmer than air at night, so aquatic retreat can aid thermoregulation, but crocodilian nighttime habitat use is variable and not explained solely by temperature.
Bees enzymatically transform collected floral nectar or other plant secretions into honey; honey is not atmospheric dew deposited for collection.

Prepubertal castration prevents typical voice deepening and reduces androgen-dependent body hair and male-pattern baldness, but absolute claims such as never growing later hair or never balding admit exceptions.
Embryonic structures differentiate in an ordered sequence; organs and visible parts are not all preformed at conception.
Many mobile animals are simultaneous or sequential hermaphrodites, while many plants have separate male and female individuals.
Some smooth-hound sharks are placentally viviparous, with a yolk-sac placenta and fetal membranes supporting embryos after yolk is depleted.
Fishes possess functional hearing, balance, smell, taste and mechanosensory systems even though external ears and nostril anatomy differ from terrestrial vertebrates.
Some congenital disorders can be inherited, but acquired mutilations, scars and pimples are not transmitted as such; the compound generalization is false.
Female-biased size dimorphism is common across many insect groups because fecundity favors larger females, though it is far from universal.
Egg shape does not determine a chick's sex; in birds sex is set genetically at fertilization.
Claw asymmetry varies among crustacean species and individuals; right-handedness may be common in some taxa but is not invariant, and lobsters also show functional asymmetry.

Domestic dog gestation is typically about 63 days from ovulation, with a relatively narrow viable range, though apparent mating-to-birth intervals and occasional viable shorter pregnancies weaken 'never.'
Hyenas have separate sexes; the female spotted hyena's enlarged clitoris and fused labia closely resemble male external genitalia and caused historical confusion.
Normal human semen is whitish or gray-white regardless of population; population-level skin pigmentation does not make it black.
Fetal orientation and normal presentation differ among species, and breech or other presentations occur; many nonhuman mammals are commonly born in positions not captured by this universal rule.
Cetaceans are placental mammals and give birth to live young after internal gestation.
Octopuses rapidly alter chromatophores, texture and posture for camouflage during hunting and in defensive responses.
Lions have the usual series of cervical vertebrae rather than a neck made from one bone.
Many small, short-lived birds breed in their first year, although numerous large or long-lived species delay maturity.
Many eagles defend large breeding territories and juveniles disperse, but they do not exclude all other birds and expulsion of offspring is not the sole cause of dispersal.
In avian embryos the early heart appears as a beating blood-filled structure and establishes major vessels, though the simplified count of exactly two vessels is stage-dependent.
Cranes undertake long migrations between Eurasian breeding grounds and African wintering areas, but the precise route to a supposed Nile source is geographically and taxonomically over-specific.
Bees compensate for wind through flight control and behavior; there is no credible general behavior of carrying stones as ballast.
Females are larger in many sharks and many fish species, often due to fecundity selection, but male-biased size and little dimorphism are also widespread, so the broad generalization is doubtful.
Sperm production commonly begins during puberty around the early teens, but males can be fertile well before twenty-one, so the compound timing claim is false.
Hens and geese can ovulate and lay unfertilized eggs without ever mating; these eggs do not reflect stored remnants of earlier fertilization.
Acquired mutilations are generally not inherited, and offspring resemblance to either parent is variable.
Dogs, wolves and some other carnivorans are born with closed eyes, but lions and various other many-toed quadrupeds make the universal grouping anatomically and biologically unreliable.
During the pupal stage of complete metamorphosis, insects generally do not feed or defecate, relying on stored reserves while tissues reorganize.
Human cranial sutures follow the same basic pattern in women and men; this claimed sex-specific count is anatomically false.
Across many animal groups larger, longer-lived species tend to produce fewer offspring per reproductive bout than small species, but ecology and life history create many exceptions.
Anglerfishes use a modified dorsal spine bearing a lure to attract prey while remaining camouflaged near the substrate.
Several fishes and some invertebrates are internally viviparous while obtaining oxygen through gills or other aquatic respiratory surfaces rather than breathing air.

The heart and vascular system are among the earliest functioning organs in vertebrate embryos and organize early circulation, but saying it is distinctly first in all blooded animals overstates diverse developmental sequences.
Other primates and some mammals produce laughter-like vocalizations and respond behaviorally to tickling, so neither trait is uniquely human.
